{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
{{technical|date=February 2024}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Farrell–Markushevich theorem''', proved independently by O. J. Farrell (1899–1981)<ref>Orin J. Farrell received his PhD (under [[Joseph L. Walsh|J. L. Walsh]]) from Harvard University in 1930 and spent his career from 1931 at [[Union College]] with a leave of absence from January 1949 to May 1949 at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. See {{MathGenealogy|id=35899|name=Orin J. Farrell}}; {{cite web|title=A History of the Mathematics Department|website=Union College|year=1993|author=Bick, Theodore A.|url=https://www.union.edu/mathematics/history-mathematics-department}}; {{cite web|title=Orin J. Farrell|website=Institute for Advanced Study|date=9 December 2019 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/orin-j-farrell}}</ref> and [[A. I. Markushevich]] (1908–1979) in 1934, is a result concerning the approximation in mean square of [[holomorphic function]]s on a bounded open set in the [[complex plane]] by complex polynomials. It states that complex polynomials form a dense subspace of the [[Bergman space]] of a domain  bounded by a simple closed [[Jordan curve]]. The [[Gram–Schmidt process]] can be used to construct an orthonormal basis in the Bergman space  and hence an explicit form of the [[Bergman kernel]], which in turn yields an explicit [[Riemann mapping theorem|Riemann mapping function]] for the domain.

==Proof==
Let Ω be the bounded Jordan domain and let  Ω<sub>''n''</sub> be bounded Jordan domains decreasing to Ω, with Ω<sub>''n''</sub> containing the closure of  Ω<sub>''n'' + 1</sub>. By the Riemann mapping theorem there is a conformal mapping ''f''<sub>''n''</sub> of Ω<sub>''n''</sub> onto  Ω, normalised to fix a given point in Ω with positive derivative there. By the [[Carathéodory kernel theorem]] ''f''<sub>''n''</sub>(''z'') converges uniformly on compacta in Ω to ''z''.<ref>See:
*{{harvnb|Conway|2000|pp=150–151}}
*{{harvnb|Markushevich|1967|pp=31–35}}
</ref> In fact Carathéodory's theorem implies that the inverse maps tend uniformly on compacta to ''z''. Given a subsequence of ''f''<sub>''n''</sub>, it has a subsequence, convergent on compacta in Ω. Since the inverse functions converge to ''z'', it follows that the subsequence converges to ''z'' on compacta. Hence  ''f''<sub>''n''</sub> converges to ''z'' on compacta in Ω.

As a consequence the derivative of ''f''<sub>''n''</sub> tends to 1 uniformly on compacta.

Let ''g'' be a square integrable holomorphic function on  Ω, i.e. an element of the Bergman space A<sup>2</sup>(Ω). Define ''g''<sub>''n''</sub> on Ω<sub>''n''</sub> by ''g''<sub>''n''</sub>(''z'') = ''g''(''f''<sub>''n''</sub>(''z''))''f''<sub>''n''</sub>'(''z''). By change of variable

:<math>\displaystyle{\|g_n\|^2_{\Omega_n} =\|g\|_\Omega^2.}</math>

Let ''h''<sub>''n''</sub> be the restriction of ''g''<sub>''n''</sub> to Ω. Then the norm of ''h''<sub>''n''</sub> is less than that of ''g''<sub>''n''</sub>. Thus these norms  are uniformly bounded. Passing to a subsequence if necessary, it can therefore be assumed that ''h''<sub>''n''</sub> has a weak limit in A<sup>2</sup>(Ω). On the other hand, ''h''<sub>''n''</sub> tends uniformly on compacta
to ''g''. Since the evaluation maps are continuous linear functions on  A<sup>2</sup>(Ω), ''g'' is the weak limit of ''h''<sub>''n''</sub>. On the other hand, by [[Runge's theorem]],  ''h''<sub>''n''</sub> lies in the closed subspace ''K'' of ''A''<sup>2</sup>(Ω) generated by complex polynomials. Hence ''g'' lies in the weak closure of ''K'', which is ''K'' itself.<ref>{{harvnb|Conway|2000|pp=151–152}}</ref>
